transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
The midterm elections were held three days ago and two U.S. Senate races are still outstanding.
One is in Alaska, where Democratic challenger Mary Peltola has a slight lead over Republican
incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan.
The other outstanding Senate race is in Mississippi. Democratic challenger Scott Colombe has a
nearly 2,000-vote lead over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.
Reporter Elise Catrine Gregg is with the Gulf States newsroom and Mississippi Public Radio.
She says vote counting will take a few more days.
We're waiting for the mail-in ballots.
Mississippi law allows mail-in ballots that are postmarked by or on Election Day to arrive
up to five business days after polls close.
So that would be Tuesday.
We're also waiting on affidavit or provisional ballots, people who may have had issues at
the polls with IDs or who may not have shown up on voter rolls.
They fill out a ballot and also have five business days to bring an ID or any other
needed info.
Now, much of this uncounted vote seems to be in more heavily populated counties.
Think around the Jackson metro area.
Elise Catrine Gregg reporting.
Republicans in Texas are reeling after losing statewide races up and down the ballot this
week.
NPR's Ashley Lopez reports many are trying to figure out next steps.
Artemio Muniz is the co-founder of the Texas Federation of Hispanic Republicans.
He says for the GOP to win some power back in the coming election cycles, leaders are
going to have to repair the party's relationship with Latino voters.
Muniz says anti-immigrant policies in the last decade have done serious damage with this
big chunk of Texas' population.
Now Texas is at a crucial juncture.
It's going to have to make up its mind.
And the good thing about Texas is that there are plenty of Republicans out there that understand
this.
Since election night, some GOP leaders have said they believe the party didn't govern
far enough to the right, setting up a struggle on the party moving forward.
Ashley Lopez, NPR News.
The Associated Press has called the mayoral race in Los Angeles, California.
It's for City Council member Nithya Raman, a Democratic socialist.
From LAist in Los Angeles, Frank Stoltz has more.
The 45-year-old Raman is a Harvard and MIT-educated urban planner whose election represents a
turn to the left for the nation's second largest city.
She overcame opposition from much of the establishment, including the Democratic Party, the Chamber
of Commerce, and many of the city's largest labor unions.
Incumbent mayor Karen Bass was deeply unpopular.
Voters are angry at a continuing homelessness crisis, the lack of affordable housing, and
a paucity of basic city services like streetlight repair.
Frustrations with her leadership became national news after deadly wildfires devastated parts
of LA last year.
For NPR News, I'm Frank Stoltz in Los Angeles.
You're listening to NPR.
First Lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian officials at the White House yesterday
after they recognized a limited temporary cease-fire she helped broker in Ukraine.
And NPR's Franco Artonez reports.
The administration is touting the recent pause around the city of Eleshky as a diplomatic
breakthrough as they ramp up efforts to secure an agreement to end the war in Ukraine.
Melania Trump said she hopes the agreement can serve as a spark that leads to something
more enduring.
We have chosen humanity over war.
Undeniably, the lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war.
The six-day pause in fighting allowed humanitarian aid to reach residents as well as allow hundreds
to be evacuated, Franco, Ordonez, NPR News, the White House.
Lawmakers in Paraguay have opened impeachment hearings into President Santiago Pena.
He is offered to resign after a bank that he was linked with collapsed.
Millions of people in Paraguay now do not have access to their savings.
The U.S. government says that hiring soared in October.
The Labor Department says employers created 165,000 new jobs last month, far more than
analysts had expected.
The industries that saw the biggest growth were in health care, transportation and professional
services.
There were also increases in average wages that Americans earned.
These were up 3.1 percent last month.
It's not clear if they're enough to keep up with inflation.
This is NPR.

topics.text: Mississippi Senate race still uncounted as Democrat Scott Colombe leads Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith by nearly 2,000 votes
Alaska Senate race unresolved, with Democrat Mary Peltola slightly ahead of Republican Dan Sullivan
Texas Republicans reeling after statewide losses, debate how to win back Latino voters
AP calls Los Angeles mayoral race for Democratic socialist council member Nithya Raman
First Lady Melania Trump hosts Russian and Ukrainian officials after brokered temporary cease-fire around Ukrainian city
Paraguay lawmakers open impeachment hearings into President Santiago Pena after bank collapse
US employers add 165,000 jobs in October, far above analyst expectations; wages rise 3.1%
